migrationNotes: Spine: a bicycle passes motion along in stages and the rates of the stages multiply; a formula with one expression inside another has the same two stages, so its derivative is the outer rate at the inner value times the inner rate.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): cal-a-rate-inside-a-rate-10 (a bare multiplication of two given rates; the idea is covered by the bicycle and the skill check).

lesson.title: A function inside a function

lead.text: Suppose you are paid £15 an hour, and each pound buys 1.2 euros. Your pay is a rate of 15 pounds per hour, and the exchange is a rate of 1.2 euros per pound. Together, 15 × 1.2 = 18 euros arrive for each hour you work.

The hours came first and the euros last, with pounds as the stage in between. To get the rate from hours to euros we multiplied the rates of the two stages. The units show why: euros per pound times pounds per hour leaves euros per hour, because the pounds cancel.
This holds for any chain of stages, and it is what the pedals and the wheel do on a bicycle. The distance covered per second is the product of the rate at each stage.

diagram.alt: A chain from hours worked to pounds earned to euros received. The first stage pays £15 per hour and the second exchanges 1.2 euros per pound. Together the chain gives 18 euros per hour.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to see each stage on its own and then the two together.

reveal.text: You multiplied the three rates: 1 × 3 × 2 = 6 metres each second. Each stage multiplies what the one before it produced.

lead.text: The same structure appears in a formula. In f(x) = (4x + 5)² there are two stages. The inner function u = 4x + 5 turns x into a number, and the outer function u² squares that number. Move x up by 1 and u moves up by 4, so the inner stage has rate 4.

The outer stage squares u, and by the power rule its rate is 2u. That rate depends on the current value of u, so it has to be measured at the value the inner stage has produced. Multiplying the two rates gives the rate of the whole formula.
This is the chain rule: the outer rate, taken at the inner value, times the inner rate.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two graphs by sliding the tangent along each. The slope of (4x + 5)² is four times the slope of (x + 5)² at the same x, because the inner stage of the first runs four times as fast as x and the inner stage of the second keeps pace with it.

workedSteps.text: Name the inner function. At x = 1 it equals 1.
The outer function, u², changes at rate 2u.
The inner function changes at 4 per unit of x.

lead.text: Same moves: name the inner function, find both rates, multiply. This time the inside is 2x + 1.

reveal.text: You took the outer rate at the inner value, then multiplied by how fast the inside moves. Without the second factor the answer would be too small.

lead.text: The inner rate can be negative. Take f(x) = (4 − x)². The inner function u = 4 − x goes down by 1 when x goes up by 1, so its rate is −1. The outer rate is still 2u, and the product is 2(4 − x) × (−1) = −2(4 − x).

The minus sign has a meaning. For x below 4 the bracket is positive, so the derivative is negative and the curve falls as x rises. At x = 4 the bracket is zero, so the slope is zero and the graph is flat at the bottom of its dip. Beyond 4 the derivative turns positive.

afterFigure.text: The pictures show (4 − x)² before and after its lowest point. Slide the tangent and watch it tilt down on the left and up on the right.

workedSteps.text: Multiply by the inner rate, then put in x = 1.

lead.text: Say the rates out loud: the outer rate at the inside, then the inner rate.

reveal.text: The 6 is 2 × 3: the outer rate's 2 times the inner rate of 3, kept beside the inner expression 3x + 1.

lead.text: Chains of rates are not limited to formulas written in x. Suppose a square patch of mould has a side of s centimetres, and the side grows at 2 centimetres a day. The area is A = s², which by the power rule changes at 2s square centimetres for each centimetre of side.

When the side is 10 cm, the area changes at 2 × 10 = 20 square centimetres per centimetre of side, and the side grows at 2 centimetres per day. So the area grows at 20 × 2 = 40 square centimetres per day, and the two rates have multiplied just as they did for the pedals and the wheel.
The pattern needs only that one quantity depends on a second, and the second on a third. The rate of the first with respect to the third is then the product of the two stage rates.

diagram.alt: A chain from days to the side of a square patch of mould to its area. The side grows at 2 centimetres a day and the area grows at 2s square centimetres per centimetre of side. At a side of 10 cm the area grows at 20 × 2 = 40 square centimetres a day.
diagram.caption: The side grows with the days and the area grows with the side. The two rates multiply.

lead.text: A cube this time. You can check any answer by expanding (x + 2)³ and differentiating term by term: the two routes must agree.

reveal.text: Expanding gives x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8, whose derivative at 1 agrees with the chain rule. Two routes, one number.

lesson.orientation: Multiply outer and inner rates when differentiating a composition.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bicycle passes your effort along in stages. The pedals turn, the chain makes the back wheel turn faster than the pedals, and the wheel rolls the bike forward. Change any one stage and the speed changes.

To find the bike's speed you do not need to know how each stage works inside. You need the rate of each: how many wheel turns come from one pedal turn, and how many metres one wheel turn covers. The speed is those rates combined.

The same structure turns up in formulas. When one expression sits inside another, as in (4x + 5)², the power rule alone gives the wrong slope. This lesson shows how to combine the rates of the two stages, and uses the bicycle to explain why.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row joined by arrows: pedal turns, wheel turns and metres travelled. The first arrow is labelled wheel turns per pedal turn and the second metres per wheel turn.
diagram.caption: Each arrow is the rate of one stage. The bike's speed depends on both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll differentiate a function inside a function by multiplying the outer rate by the inner rate.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every real formula is a function inside a function.

recap.keyIdea: Rates in a chain multiply: differentiate the outer function at the inner value, then multiply by the inner function's rate.

blocks.text: Back on the bicycle, you found that it covers 6 metres each second by multiplying 1 × 3 × 2. You used the same multiplication to get 8 for (4x − 3)² at x = 1, and you saw a falling inside turn the slope negative.

recap.nextHook: Derivatives measure rates, and the commonest rate is speed. The next lesson follows a moving object through its position, velocity and acceleration.

hints: Multiply the outer rate by the inner rate.
The derivative is the outer square's rate multiplied by the slope of the inner line.
Evaluate the inner expression, then multiply by both rate factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain rule gives 2(2x + 1) × 2. At 1 the result is 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Outer rate 2(2x + 1) = 6 at x = 1, times the inner rate 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 is the outer rate only. Multiply by how fast the inside changes as well.

hints: The inner expression decreases as x increases.
The derivative of the inner expression is negative.
Multiply twice the inner expression by its signed rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The derivative is 2(3 − x) × (−1); at 1 it equals −4.

questions.onCorrect: −4. The outer rate is 4, and the inside falls as x grows, so multiply by −1.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the inner rate: 3 − x falls as x grows, so it is negative.

hints: Count both stages of the change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative of the square is evaluated at 3x + 1, then multiplied by the inner derivative 3.

questions.onCorrect: 6(3x + 1). Twice the inner value, times the inner rate 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 2(3x + 1) is only the outer rate. Multiply by how fast 3x + 1 changes.
The inner expression stays inside the bracket. 3x + 1 is not differentiated on its own.

hints: The inner rate is one.
The derivative of a cube is three times the square of its input.
Square the inner value before multiplying by both rate factors.
questions.onCorrect: 27. Outer rate 3(x + 2)² at x = 1, times the inner rate 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Square the inner value, 3, then multiply by the power.
3 is the power. The outer rate is 3 times the square of the inner value.

hints: There is an inner factor as well as the cubic power.
The outer rate is three times the square of the inner expression.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner line after evaluating its squared value.
questions.onCorrect: 54. Outer rate 3(2x − 1)² = 27, times the inner rate 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 is the outer rate only. Multiply by the inner rate, 2.
18 is 2 × 9. The outer rate has a 3 in front of the squared inner value.

questions.prompt: Why is differentiating only the outer function insufficient for a composition?
hints: Follow the change through both functions.

acceptedIdeas: The inner input may change at a different rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The chain rule accounts for how rapidly the inner input changes with x.

choices.label: The inner input may change at a different rate
Every composition has a constant slope
The outer derivative must be added to the original function

questions.onCorrect: The inside has its own rate. The chain rule multiplies the outer rate by it.

misconceptions.feedback: A composition's slope is not constant. The outer rate depends on the inner value.
Rates in a chain multiply. Nothing is added to the original function.

questions.prompt: A bike's pedals turn once each second. The wheel makes 3 turns for every pedal turn, and each wheel turn carries the bike 2 metres. How far does the bike travel each second, in metres?
hints: How many wheel turns happen in one second?
Three wheel turns per second. How far does each carry the bike?
Multiply the wheel turns per second by the metres per turn.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 pedal turn per second × 3 wheel turns per pedal turn × 2 m per wheel turn = 6 m each second.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Rates chained one inside the next multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is the wheel turns each second. Each of those carries the bike further.
The rates are chained, so they multiply. Adding them mixes up different units.

questions.prompt: In the worked line for (4x − 3)², why multiply by 4 at the end?
hints: How fast does 4x − 3 change when x increases by 1?

acceptedIdeas: The inside changes 4 times as fast as x
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: u = 4x − 3 changes 4 times as fast as x, so the outer rate has to be scaled by 4.

choices.label: The inside changes 4 times as fast as x
4 is the power of the square

questions.onCorrect: The inside changes 4 times as fast as x, and that speed carries through to the whole function.

misconceptions.feedback: The power is 2, and it has already been used in the outer rate.
The sign comes from the rates themselves. Here the 4 says how quickly the inside moves.

questions.prompt: A square's side is s = 3t centimetres after t seconds, so its area is A = s². How fast is the area growing at t = 2, in cm² per second?
hints: First find the side at t = 2.
How fast does A = s² change per unit of s? Then how fast does s change?
Multiply the two rates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At t = 2, s = 6. The area changes at 2s = 12 per cm of side, and the side grows at 3 cm per second: 12 × 3 = 36.

questions.onCorrect: 36. The area's rate per cm of side, times how fast the side grows.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is how fast the area changes per cm of side. Multiply by how fast the side grows.
6 is the side length at t = 2, not a rate of area.

questions.prompt: The outer function changes at rate 6 at the inner value, and the inner function changes at rate 5. What is the rate of the whole function?
hints: How do rates in a chain combine?
They multiply, as with the bike gears.
What is 6 times 5?

misconceptions.feedback: Rates in a chain multiply. They are not added.

citations.claim: When one quantity depends on a second and the second on a third, the rate of the first with respect to the third is the product of the stage rates.
1 pedal turn per second × 3 wheel turns per pedal turn × 2 m per wheel turn = 6 m each second.
For f(x) = (4x + 5)² the inner function 4x + 5 has rate 4 and the outer function u² has rate 2u, so f′(x) = 8(4x + 5).
For f(x) = (4x − 3)², the outer rate 2u = 2 at x = 1 times the inner rate 4 gives f′(1) = 8.
For f(x) = (4 − x)² the inner rate is −1, so f′(x) = −2(4 − x), negative below 4 and positive above it.
The derivative of (3x + 1)² is 2(3x + 1) × 3 = 6(3x + 1).
For A = s² with s growing at a steady rate, dA/dt = 2s × ds/dt; at s = 10 and 2 cm per day the area grows at 40 cm² per day.
For f(x) = (x + 2)³, f′(x) = 3(x + 2)² × 1, so f′(1) = 27, matching the expanded form.
The chain rule gives 2(2x + 1) × 2. At 1 the result is 12.
The derivative is 2(3 − x) × (−1); at 1 it equals −4.
The derivative of the square is evaluated at 3x + 1, then multiplied by the inner derivative 3.
f′(x) = 3(x + 2)²; at 1 this gives 27.
f′(x) = 6(2x − 1)²; at 2 the rate is 6 × 9 = 54.
The chain rule accounts for how rapidly the inner input changes with x.
1 pedal turn per second × 3 wheel turns per pedal turn × 2 m per wheel turn = 6 m each second.
u = 4x − 3 changes 4 times as fast as x, so the outer rate has to be scaled by 4.
At t = 2, s = 6. The area changes at 2s = 12 per cm of side, and the side grows at 3 cm per second: 12 × 3 = 36.
2(4x + 1) × 4 gives 40 at x = 1.
